### Page: Drone dock power

URL: https://www.melrakki.systems/drone-dock-power/
Summary: Drone-in-a-box systems assume mains at the landing zone. How to engineer off-grid power for a dock: standby load, charge peaks, weather and sortie rate.

Drone dock power

#### Powering a drone dock where there is no grid.

What it takes to replace the mains connection a dock assumes with energy generated and stored on site, and why the answer depends on the dock's baseline as much as its charge peaks.

The missing layer

##### The aircraft is autonomous. The power behind it usually is not.

Drone-in-a-box systems can launch, land, recharge and re-task an aircraft with no one present. Almost all of them assume a mains connection at the landing site.

That assumption holds on a depot roof. It does not hold on a pipeline route, a remote perimeter, a border or a disaster zone, which are often the places an autonomous aircraft would be most useful. However capable the aircraft, the capability stops at the landing zone if nothing there can recharge it.

Replacing the mains connection is an off-grid power problem, and a harder one than powering a camera. It is worth understanding why before anyone specifies panels or batteries.

The dock as a load

##### A continuous baseline with a spike after every sortie.

A dock has two loads layered on top of each other.

**The baseline** runs all day and all night: the dock's control electronics, its communications link, its own backup battery, and the heating or cooling that keeps the aircraft battery and mechanism within temperature. On a cold or hot day the thermal part can grow substantially, and it runs whether or not anything flies.

**The charging peaks** arrive after every sortie. Docks are designed to turn the aircraft round quickly, so they recharge fast, which means a short, high draw.

Published specifications show the scale. One widely deployed commercial dock, for example, takes a 100 to 240 V AC mains supply with a maximum input of 800 W, and recharges its aircraft's roughly 150 Wh battery from 15% to 95% in under half an hour. It is rated to operate from −30 to 50 °C. Other docks differ, which is exactly why the real figures have to come from the dock you intend to use.

*Figure: The peaks decide how much power the storage and conversion must deliver, in the cold, at night. The baseline, running 24 hours a day, usually decides how much energy the site has to generate.*

Why this is harder than a camera

A camera mast is sized mostly for energy. A dock has to be sized for energy and for peak power: the storage and conversion must deliver the charge peak on a winter night with the battery cold and the sun long gone. It usually needs an AC supply as well, which adds conversion losses a DC camera system does not have.

Sizing

##### The sortie arithmetic.

The daily energy a dock site needs comes from three terms, and each has to be taken for the worst month rather than the average:

1. **Baseline**: the dock's standby draw, including thermal management in the site's winter or summer extreme, multiplied by 24 hours.

2. **Sorties**: the number of flights a day, multiplied by the energy to recharge the aircraft each time, grossed up for charger and conversion losses.

3. **Everything else on the node**: cameras, sensors or radios sharing the site.

The standby figure is the one most often missing from datasheets, and it is frequently the largest term because it never stops. As an illustration only, using assumed rather than measured figures: a dock idling at 50 W uses 1.2 kWh a day before anything flies, while six recharges of a battery the size of the one above add less than 1 kWh. Double the standby in a hard winter and it dominates completely. That is why compatibility has to be established by measurement on the actual dock, not by reading its maximum input.

Weather cuts both ways. The coldest weeks raise the baseline, reduce battery capacity and weaken the sun at the same time. In a northern winter, a hybrid architecture with fuelled backup is often the honest answer for a dock, the same logic that separates [Harka Solar and Harka Hybrid](https://www.melrakki.systems/harka/).

Operations

##### Where the rules sit, and what power changes.

Persistent drone operations beyond visual line of sight (BVLOS) need regulatory approval as well as power. In the UK the Civil Aviation Authority is working towards [routine BVLOS operations by 2027](https://www.caa.co.uk/drones/drone-regulations/policy-programmes/beyond-visual-line-of-sight-bvlos/), and remotely operated dock deployments are already being approved case by case. In June 2026, for example, [Network Rail was reported to have received CAA approval](https://www.dronewatch.eu/network-rail-obtains-uk-approval-for-bvlos-dji-dock-operations/) for BVLOS dock operations at two sites, flown from a remote operations centre.

Power does not grant any permission. What it changes is where a dock can go and how dependable it is once there. As approvals become routine, the constraint on where docks can be placed shifts from regulation towards infrastructure: a landing zone needs power, a communications link and protection from the weather, and a remote landing zone needs all three without a grid.

How we approach it

##### Tested combinations only.

**Compatibility is proven by test, not assumed.** Melrakki powers only dock and aircraft combinations it has tested and passed. A datasheet's maximum input tells us very little about how a dock behaves at −10 °C at three in the morning, which is the condition the power system actually has to survive. Tell us the dock you use or are considering, and we will tell you plainly where it stands.

That discipline is also why Greni exists.

In development. Prototype in field test

Melrakki Greni, MK-GR-01: an autonomous edge node for drones.

Greni is an off-grid charging and docking station built on skid-mounted solar hybrid power, with a tilting solar array and lithium storage, designed around the dock's full load: the charge peaks and the baseline that runs day and night. A working prototype is in field test with a leading UK organisation. That evaluation is confidential, and we will not publish figures or compatibilities until testing lets us stand behind them.

[Explore Greni](https://www.melrakki.systems/greni/) or [register early interest](https://www.melrakki.systems/greni/#interest) to help shape how it is specified.

What people ask

##### Common questions.

**Can a drone dock run on solar power?**

In principle, yes, if generation and storage cover the dock's daily energy in the worst month and the storage can deliver the charging peak on a cold night. In a northern winter, solar alone often cannot, and a hybrid architecture with fuelled backup is the more honest design.

**How much power does a drone dock need?**

Two figures matter. The peak is set by fast charging after each sortie; one widely deployed commercial dock, for example, lists a maximum input of 800 W. The daily energy is set mostly by the standby baseline, including heating or cooling, which runs 24 hours a day. The baseline is rarely published and has to be measured.

**Will Melrakki power the drone dock we already have?**

Only if that dock and aircraft combination has been tested and passed by Melrakki. We do not assume compatibility from a datasheet. Tell us the dock and aircraft you use and we will tell you where it stands.

**When will Greni be available?**

Greni is a working prototype in field test. We are not publishing dates, figures or compatibilities until testing lets us stand behind them. Registering interest puts your requirement in front of us while the specification is being finalised.

**Does off-grid power affect BVLOS approval?**

No. Approval concerns the operation, the airspace and the operator. Power affects where a dock can be placed and how dependable it is. The two need planning together, but one does not grant the other.

### Page: Critical infrastructure

URL: https://www.melrakki.systems/critical-infrastructure/
Summary: Remote substations, pipelines, roadside and telemetry assets often depend on the power they protect. Where autonomous power removes that dependency.

Critical infrastructure

#### Power for the edge of critical infrastructure.

The control room has resilient supplies. The camera on the far fence, the telemetry outstation and the radio on the hill often run from the same local supply as the asset they protect. When it fails, they fail with it.

The problem

##### The edge often depends on the power it is meant to protect.

Critical infrastructure does not end at the control room. It ends where the equipment has to work: the far fence of a substation, a valve on a pipeline route, a roadside cabinet, a radio link on a hill.

That edge is often powered by whatever is nearest. Very often that is the same local supply that feeds the asset being protected or monitored. When it fails, through a fault, a storm, a fire or deliberate interference, the protection fails with it, at exactly the moment it is needed. Restoring it means a site visit, in the same conditions that caused the outage.

We have written about this at length. [The last mile of resilience](https://www.melrakki.systems/resilience/the-last-mile-of-resilience/) sets out why the edge behaves differently from the centre. [When the infrastructure becomes the vulnerability](https://www.melrakki.systems/resilience/when-the-infrastructure-becomes-the-vulnerability/) looks at the dependency chain beneath protective security. [The sabotage problem](https://www.melrakki.systems/resilience/the-sabotage-problem/) asks what happens when someone is trying to make it fail. This page is the practical version: where independent power belongs, and how to decide.

*Figure: Redundancy adds a second copy of something. Independence removes the shared dependency. At remote assets the second is usually cheaper, and it is the one that survives the event that takes out the first.*

Asset by asset

##### What the edge depends on, and what fails first.

The pattern repeats across sectors. The question to ask of every remote asset is the same: if its supply went tonight, what would still be watching it?

| Remote asset | What it usually runs on | What takes it down | What autonomous power changes |
|---|---|---|---|
| Substation and switching-site perimeter | The site's own auxiliary or a nearby low-voltage supply | The fault, fire or outage the security is there to watch | Cameras and detection keep recording through the event and report it |
| Pipeline and linear routes | Nothing, or a generator at points of interest | Distance: no supply for kilometres, and fuel that has to be driven out | Surveillance and sensing at the points that matter, with nothing to deliver |
| Rail and highway roadside systems | Roadside supply along the route | Cable faults, damage and theft; supply works that take months to programme | Temporary or permanent monitoring without civil works or a supply application |
| Telemetry and monitoring outstations | Small local supply or a solar panel | Undersized winter power, and a communications link on a different supply | Power and link designed as one system, sized for the worst month |
| Remote communications nodes | Local mains with short battery backup | A prolonged outage that outlasts the backup | Days of autonomy rather than hours. See remote communications power |
| Water, reservoir and remote utility compounds | Site supply, often single feed | Storms that take out supply and access together | Protection that does not share the asset's single point of failure |

Questions to ask

##### Seven questions for any remote security or monitoring system.

These apply whoever supplies the equipment. If the answers are uncomfortable, the edge is where to start.

- What does this system draw power from, and does that supply fail with the asset it protects?

- How long does it keep working if that supply goes, measured in the worst week of the year rather than the best?

- Is the communications link that carries its alarms powered independently, or does it share the same point of failure?

- Who has to travel for it to recover, and how long would that take in the weather that caused the outage?

- Does it report that it is failing before it fails, or do you find out when it is already dark?

- If fuel is involved, who delivers it, how often, and is the fuel store itself a target?

- Could someone disconnect it deliberately, and how visible and reachable is the thing they would cut?

Context

##### Why the edge is now a resilience question, not a maintenance one.

UK government and regulators have moved steadily towards the same concern. The [UK Government Resilience Action Plan](https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/uk-government-resilience-action-plan/uk-government-resilience-action-plan-html) commits to mapping vulnerabilities and interdependencies across critical national infrastructure. The [Storm Arwen review](https://assets.publishing.service.gov.uk/government/uploads/system/uploads/attachment_data/file/1081116/storm-arwen-review-final-report.pdf) recorded supply disruption to just over a million customers in November 2021: most were restored within a day, and a small but significant number were without power for up to 13 days. The [communications industry's post-incident report](https://assets.publishing.service.gov.uk/media/62828be08fa8f556165a1dec/GOV.UK_ECRRG_Post_Incident_Report_-_2021_2022_Severe_Storms.pdf) found battery backup at mobile sites depleted after a number of hours, because it had been designed for brief outages rather than prolonged ones.

In June 2026 Ofcom's revised [network and service resilience guidance](https://www.ofcom.org.uk/internet-based-services/network-security/resilience-guidance) asked communications providers to seek to eliminate loss of key dependencies, including mains power, for a significant period of time, leaving the duration to risk assessment. The direction is consistent: the edge is expected to keep working when the supply around it does not.

Our approach

##### Power that does not share the asset's point of failure.

We start with the asset and its worst credible week, then engineer the power from the load backwards: what has to keep running, for how long, with what access, in which conditions. Where a remote supply exists but is shared with the asset, the case for independence is usually stronger than the case for a bigger backup on the same feed.

Melrakki provides the power infrastructure. The platforms are delivered open for the operator's own cameras, sensors and radios, or we specify them.

[Clean tier · MK-HK-S6 ### Harka Solar Where the worst month covers the load and nothing should be delivered to site. Silent, no fuel, no engine. Harka Solar →](https://www.melrakki.systems/harka/)[Endurance tier · MK-HK-H6 ### Harka Hybrid Where uptime must hold through midwinter. Solar first, with an HVO generator that only recharges the battery. Harka Hybrid →](https://www.melrakki.systems/harka/#specifications)[Engineered to your application ### Bespoke Multiple loads, unusual voltages, integration onto an existing asset, or conditions no standard platform was sized for. Bespoke engineering →](https://www.melrakki.systems/bespoke/)

In development  For linear assets that need an aerial look on demand, [Greni](https://www.melrakki.systems/greni/), our autonomous drone node, is a working prototype in field test.

What people ask

##### Common questions.

**Is a UPS enough for remote security equipment?**

A UPS bridges a short interruption on the same supply. It does not remove the dependency: if the outage lasts longer than the battery, or the fault is on the feed the UPS sits behind, the equipment goes dark. At remote assets, independent generation and storage sized for the worst week is usually the stronger answer.

**Which remote assets are the best candidates for autonomous power?**

Assets where mains is absent or unreliable, where the security or monitoring shares a supply with the asset it protects, and where restoring a failed system means an expensive or slow site visit. Perimeter security, linear routes, roadside systems, telemetry and remote communications nodes are the common cases.

**Does Melrakki supply the cameras and sensors?**

Melrakki provides the power infrastructure. The platforms are delivered open so operators can fit their own cameras, sensors and radios, and we can specify the payload where that helps.

**How do you decide between solar-only and hybrid power for an infrastructure site?**

By the worst month. If the site's worst-month sun covers the load with margin, solar-only removes fuel entirely. If not, a hybrid carries the load on solar and battery and runs a generator only to recharge in the deficit window. Our [guide to off-grid architectures](https://www.melrakki.systems/off-grid-power/) sets out the numbers.

Sources

##### Where the external figures come from.

1. [Cabinet Office, UK Government Resilience Action Plan, July 2025](https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/uk-government-resilience-action-plan/uk-government-resilience-action-plan-html)
2. [Energy Emergencies Executive Committee, Storm Arwen Review: Final Report, June 2022](https://assets.publishing.service.gov.uk/government/uploads/system/uploads/attachment_data/file/1081116/storm-arwen-review-final-report.pdf)
3. [Electronic Communications Resilience and Response Group, Post Incident Report: 2021/2022 Severe Storms](https://assets.publishing.service.gov.uk/media/62828be08fa8f556165a1dec/GOV.UK_ECRRG_Post_Incident_Report_-_2021_2022_Severe_Storms.pdf)
4. [Ofcom, Network and Service Resilience Guidance, June 2026](https://www.ofcom.org.uk/internet-based-services/network-security/resilience-guidance)
5. [NPSA, Critical National Infrastructure](https://www.npsa.gov.uk/about-npsa/critical-national-infrastructure)

### Page: Oil and gas

URL: https://www.melrakki.systems/oil-and-gas/
Summary: Autonomous solar and hybrid power for surveillance, monitoring and communications on remote oil and gas sites, from a team with over a decade in the sector.

Oil and gas

#### Power for oil and gas sites the grid never reached.

Wellsites, pipeline routes, laydown areas and remote perimeters need watching and connecting, often far from dependable power. The team behind Melrakki has been putting autonomous solar power into that environment for more than a decade.

The problem

##### Watching remote assets without a convoy to keep them powered.

Oil and gas assets are spread across the places the grid never reached: wellsites, pipeline routes, gathering stations, laydown yards and camp perimeters, often hours from the nearest dependable supply.

They still need watching, connecting and monitoring. The usual answer is a generator at each point, and on an oil and gas site that answer carries costs a spreadsheet tends to miss. Every fuel run is a vehicle journey on remote roads, which is an exposure in its own right. Every fuel store is something to be stolen or diverted. Every running engine is noise, heat and exhaust at a site where people may be trying to see or hear what is happening.

The climate adds its own pressure: long, deep winters and extreme summer heat, dust and wind, and service intervals set by access rather than convenience.

Applications

##### Where autonomous power earns its place on an oil and gas site.

Melrakki's experience in the sector is surveillance-led. The same load-backwards method applies to any remote load on the site.

| Where power is needed | What it carries | What matters most |
|---|---|---|
| Wellsite and pad perimeters | Cameras, infrared, detection, a cellular or satellite link | Continuous recording through winter nights; nothing on site worth stealing |
| Pipeline routes and points of interest | Surveillance at crossings, valves and access points; sensing | No supply for kilometres; long unattended intervals |
| Laydown yards and construction compounds | Perimeter cameras, lighting, access monitoring | Rapid deployment before permanent power exists; relocation as work moves |
| Gates, camps and access roads | Surveillance, communications relays | Dependable uptime without adding to the fuel logistics |
| Instrumentation and monitoring | Low-power sensing and telemetry | Power and communications designed together |

The hazardous-area boundary

##### Power stands outside the zone.

Hazardous areas

Harka platforms are not certified for use inside hazardous areas. A solar array, a battery and, on the Hybrid, a generator are all potential ignition sources, and none of them is rated for an explosive atmosphere.

Platforms must be sited outside classified zones, as defined by the operator's hazardous area classification. In Great Britain that falls under DSEAR, with equipment for explosive atmospheres covered by ATEX and UKEX; internationally, IECEx. Where monitoring is needed inside a zone, certified equipment in the zone can be powered from a platform sited safely outside it, subject to the operator's own design and approval.

The zone drawing is therefore one of the first documents we ask for. It decides where power can stand, how far cable runs to certified equipment have to go, and sometimes whether a camera can see what it needs to from outside the boundary. For the regulatory background, see HSE's guidance on [ATEX and explosive atmospheres](https://www.hse.gov.uk/fireandexplosion/atex.htm) and on [hazardous area classification](https://www.hse.gov.uk/comah/sragtech/techmeasareaclas.htm).

Climate

##### Designing for the extremes the site will actually see.

Oil and gas sites tend to sit at the extremes, and the power system feels every one of them.

- **Cold** cuts what a battery can deliver. EnerSys data for pure-lead AGM shows available capacity falling to about 84% at 0 °C and 65% at −20 °C at high discharge rates. Battery enclosures are insulated to the site's winter.

- **Heat** shortens battery life: EnerSys gives lead-acid life halving for roughly every 8 to 10 °C above 20 to 25 °C. Enclosures are ventilated and shaded to the site's summer.

- **Dust and soiling** quietly reduce solar yield. The cleaning interval belongs in the design, alongside the worst-month sun figure.

- **Wind** loading on the mast and array is engineered to each site's requirement.

- **Winter sun** at northern latitudes may not cover the load at all. That is what the Hybrid tier is for.

We do not publish a single operating temperature range for Harka because the thermal design is specified per site: insulated, ventilated, or both, to the conditions the customer needs it to survive.

Fuel

##### Less fuel to deliver, store and protect.

On a remote oil and gas site, fuel is not just an operating cost. It is a logistics chain, a security problem and a safety exposure.

**Harka Solar** removes it entirely: no fuel, no engine, nothing to deliver, nothing to steal. Where the worst month's sun covers the load, it runs with no resupply at all.

**Harka Hybrid** minimises it. Solar and battery carry the load; a Stage V generator running on HVO renewable diesel starts only when the battery reaches 40% state of charge, recharges it and stops. From a 125-litre HVO tank, at the 100 W reference load, it runs up to 1,840 hours, around eleven weeks, before refuelling, with most of the fuel burned in the weeks the sun cannot cover.

The full argument, including when a generator is still the right answer, is in [the true cost of a diesel generator on a remote site](https://www.melrakki.systems/resilience/the-true-cost-of-a-diesel-generator/).

Experience

Solar surveillance infrastructure across 58 oil and gas sites in Kazakhstan.

The team behind Melrakki has spent more than a decade designing and deploying off-grid solar surveillance into demanding sectors, and oil and gas is where much of that experience was earned: solar CCTV infrastructure co-designed for 58 sites in Kazakhstan, where continental winters and summers are both severe, alongside work in highways, construction and critical infrastructure. It is the reason we size for the worst credible week, not the best day.

[More about Melrakki](https://www.melrakki.systems/about/).

Platforms

##### Autonomous power for the remote edge of the field.

What people ask

##### Common questions.

**Can a Harka platform be installed inside an ATEX zone?**

No. Harka platforms are not certified for hazardous areas and must be sited outside classified zones, as set by the operator's hazardous area classification. Certified equipment inside a zone can be powered from a platform outside it, subject to the operator's design and approval.

**Will solar power work in extreme heat and cold?**

Yes, when the system is designed for it. Cold reduces battery capacity and winter reduces solar yield, so the system is sized for the worst month; heat shortens battery life, so enclosures are ventilated and shaded. Insulation and ventilation are specified to each site's conditions rather than to a single published range.

**Solar only or hybrid for a remote wellsite?**

Let the worst month decide. If the site's worst-month sun covers the load with margin, Harka Solar removes fuel from the site entirely. If not, Harka Hybrid carries the load on solar and battery and runs its HVO generator only to recharge the battery when it reaches 40% state of charge.

**How are the platforms transported to remote sites?**

Harka platforms are skid-mounted with forklift pockets, travel ten to a truck and are built for all-terrain transport. One person raises the mast manually without tools, and the solar array opens by hand.

---

### Page: Defence and security

URL: https://www.melrakki.systems/defence-and-security/
Summary: Off-grid power for surveillance and communications that reduces fuel logistics and signature: acoustic, thermal, exhaust, and the resupply pattern itself.

Defence and security

#### Autonomous power for defence and security sites.

For surveillance and communications at a perimeter, a border or a temporary compound, the power system decides more than uptime. It decides what the site sounds like, how it looks to a thermal camera, and how often someone has to drive to it.

The problem

##### Power that adds a logistics chain and a signature to the site it protects.

Persistent surveillance and communications at a perimeter, a border or a temporary compound depend on power, and the way that power is delivered has consequences beyond uptime.

A generator can be heard, seen on a thermal camera and smelt downwind. Its fuel has to be delivered, and every delivery is a vehicle on a predictable route to a known point. Its fuel store is worth stealing. None of this matters much on a secure, accessible site. At the edge, it can matter more than the equipment the generator is powering.

Military analysis has made the same point about logistics for years. A [2025 RUSI commentary](https://www.rusi.org/explore-our-research/publications/commentary/achieving-military-advantage-british-army-through-energy-transition) on energy in the British Army recalls estimates that it took around 27 litres of fuel to deliver one litre to a patrol base in southern Afghanistan, and that 52% of casualties in that campaign were sustained maintaining lines of communication and resupply. It also notes that vehicle acoustic signatures can be detected and identified at 10 km. The scale of a fixed security site is different. The principle is not: **every delivery is an exposure, and every running engine is a signature.**

The signature ledger

##### What each architecture gives away.

| Signature | Diesel generator site | Harka Hybrid | Harka Solar |
|---|---|---|---|
| Acoustic | An engine running continuously | Silent on battery. A low-rpm, noise-insulated generator runs only to recharge | Silent. No engine |
| Thermal | Engine block and exhaust heat | No engine heat on battery; generator heat while recharging | No engine heat or exhaust. With appropriate insulation, the electronics' heat signature is extremely low |
| Exhaust | Continuous | Only while recharging, on HVO | None |
| Resupply pattern | Regular fuel runs to a known point | Up to 1,840 h between refuelling at 100 W | None: nothing to deliver |
| Visual | Generator, fuel store, vehicle tracks | Mast, array and generator housing | Mast and array |

Two honest limits. First, a 6 m mast and a solar array are visible: lowering the acoustic, thermal and logistic signature is not concealment, and siting still matters. Second, the Hybrid is only silent while the sun and battery are carrying the load. Its generator runs only when the battery falls to 40% state of charge, which from a full battery at 100 W is roughly 31 hours of silent running before any solar top-up. Where signature is the overriding requirement, the load and the array are sized so the generator runs as rarely as possible, or the clean tier is used.

Logistics

##### Fewer visits, by design.

For a security site, the number of times someone must visit is a design input, not an operating detail. It sets the battery reserve, the fuel endurance and whether remote monitoring is essential or optional.

- **Reserve** should cover the longest credible interval before anyone can attend, in the worst week of the year. Harka holds 75 h (Solar) and 41 h (Hybrid) on battery at 100 W; lighter loads hold proportionally longer.

- **Endurance** is unlimited on Harka Solar wherever the worst month's sun covers the load, and up to 1,840 h before refuelling on Harka Hybrid at 100 W, from a 125-litre HVO tank.

- **Knowing the site is healthy** without going there takes remote monitoring, which is optional on Harka and usually worth specifying where visits are costly or exposed.

- **Deployment** is deliberately simple: skid-mounted platforms with forklift pockets, ten to a truck, a manual mast one person raises in minutes without tools, and an array that opens by hand.

Resilience

##### Harder to disconnect.

Independent power is also a resilience measure. A camera that runs from the same supply as the site it protects can be switched off by anyone who can reach that supply. One that generates and stores its own power, with no external cable to cut and its sensitive components in a lockable steel bay, is harder to disconnect.

That does not make it invulnerable, and we do not claim it does. It removes one dependency, which is usually the cheapest one to remove. The fuller argument is in [the sabotage problem](https://www.melrakki.systems/resilience/the-sabotage-problem/) and [when the infrastructure becomes the vulnerability](https://www.melrakki.systems/resilience/when-the-infrastructure-becomes-the-vulnerability/).

Platforms

##### Power specified by the mission, not the catalogue.

[Clean tier · MK-HK-S6 ### Harka Solar The lowest signature in the range: no engine, no fuel, no exhaust. For sites where the worst month's sun covers the load. Harka Solar →](https://www.melrakki.systems/harka/)[Endurance tier · MK-HK-H6 ### Harka Hybrid For higher latitudes, winter and heavier loads, with a generator that runs only to recharge and long intervals between refuelling. Harka Hybrid →](https://www.melrakki.systems/harka/#specifications)[Engineered to your application ### Bespoke Constraints on size, weight, portability, signature or mounting that the design has to be built around. Bespoke engineering →](https://www.melrakki.systems/bespoke/)

Wind loading, insulation and ventilation are engineered to each site's requirement. For camera load budgets and winter sizing, see [solar-powered surveillance](https://www.melrakki.systems/solar-powered-surveillance/); for the architecture choices in general, [off-grid power systems for remote sites](https://www.melrakki.systems/off-grid-power/).

Melrakki does not publish customer or programme information, and nothing on this page implies a defence approval, accreditation or contract. We engineer to the requirement and say plainly what is proven and what is not.

What people ask

##### Common questions.

**Is solar power silent?**

Harka Solar has no engine and makes no operating noise. Harka Hybrid is silent while the sun and battery carry the load; its low-rpm, noise-insulated generator runs only to recharge the battery when it reaches 40% state of charge.

**Does a solar platform have a thermal signature?**

There is no engine heat or exhaust. The electronics still produce some heat, and with appropriate insulation that signature is extremely low. The mast and array remain visible, so siting still matters.

**How long can a site run without resupply?**

Harka Solar needs no resupply wherever the worst month's sun covers the load, and holds 75 hours on battery alone at 100 W. Harka Hybrid holds 41 hours on battery and runs up to 1,840 hours before refuelling at 100 W. Lighter loads extend all three figures.

**How quickly can a platform be deployed?**

Harka platforms are skid-mounted, travel ten to a truck and are moved by forklift. One person raises the mast manually in minutes without tools, and the solar array opens by hand.

**Does Melrakki hold defence approvals?**

We do not publish customer or programme information and make no claim to defence approvals or accreditations on this site. Tell us the requirement and we will be straight about what is proven and what would need to be established.

Sources

## Part 3. Field notes

Essays by the founder, Simon Legrand. They explain Melrakki's thinking and cite external sources. They are not product specifications. Read the full notes at the links.

---

### When the grid goes away

URL: https://www.melrakki.systems/resilience/when-the-grid-goes-away/
Published: 2026-09-23

What happens to a remote camera, sensor or comms node when its power disappears. Key points: every remote capability depends on power, so power is 'infrastructure for other infrastructure'. 'The grid goes away' means no connection at all, or one that cannot be relied on when needed. A generator is a resilience component with its own dependency chain (fuel, transport, servicing, access), not a definition of resilience. Redundancy (a second copy) differs from independence (not depending on the thing that failed). Good design moves the dependency boundary rather than claiming absolute independence. Systems are sized for the worst credible week (low sun, cold, snow, wind, heavier load, repeated demand, no one able to attend), which differs site by site. The note also floats 'autonomous resilience infrastructure' as a direction, stating that Melrakki does not claim to run such a network today.

---

### The last mile of resilience

URL: https://www.melrakki.systems/resilience/the-last-mile-of-resilience/
Published: 2026-09-25

Critical infrastructure is only as resilient as its furthest node. Uses the Storm Arwen reviews (2021) and Ofcom's mobile power resilience work as evidence that the edge recovers more slowly than the centre. Distinguishes redundancy, diversity, independence and recovery. Gives Melrakki's working definition of autonomous edge infrastructure ('infrastructure designed to maintain critical functions at remote locations with reduced dependence on external power, logistics, communications and routine human attendance'), explicitly not an established industry category or a Melrakki invention. It has five layers: energy autonomy, operational autonomy, communications resilience, physical autonomy and mission autonomy. Power is the enabling layer, and that is where Melrakki works.

---

### When the infrastructure becomes the vulnerability

URL: https://www.melrakki.systems/resilience/when-the-infrastructure-becomes-the-vulnerability/
Published: 2026-09-25

A security system can be technically robust and operationally fragile if it depends on infrastructure outside its control. Uses the March 2025 North Hyde substation fire, with NESO's finding of a transformer bushing failure and police finding nothing suspicious, as an example of a dependency failure rather than a security story. Argues for asking what the protection itself depends on, and for moving the dependency boundary closer to the asset. Cites NPSA, NCSC, MI5, Cabinet Office and NESO sources.

---

### The sabotage problem

URL: https://www.melrakki.systems/resilience/the-sabotage-problem/
Published: 2026-09-25

Security asks whether an attack can be stopped; resilience asks whether the system can continue if it happens. Sets out what UK and NATO sources document about state-linked sabotage (the National Security Strategy 2025, the National Security (State Threats) Act 2026, MI5 statements, NATO's 2026 Resilience Baseline Requirements). It also states what they do not claim: no specific attack is predicted at any site, and most infrastructure faults are accidental. Discusses the dependency cascade, shared dependencies as single points of failure, and designing remote infrastructure to be harder to disconnect.

---

### When the drone has its own power station

URL: https://www.melrakki.systems/resilience/off-grid-drone-infrastructure/
Published: 2026-09-23

A drone can only be as autonomous as the infrastructure behind it. Most drone-in-a-box systems assume mains power at the dock, so persistent remote operation is an energy problem. Describes Greni as a prototype in confidential field test, with no results, endurance figures or compatibilities to report. Covers the operating loop (persistent readiness, not persistent flight), weather and hybrid sizing, and the UK regulatory context: BVLOS in the Specific category under UK SORA since April 2025, the Atypical Air Environment policy and the CAA roadmap towards routine BVLOS by 2027. States that an off-grid node exempts no one from airspace, protective-security or data-protection obligations.

---

### The true cost of a diesel generator on a remote site

URL: https://www.melrakki.systems/resilience/the-true-cost-of-a-diesel-generator/
Published: 2026-09-23

On a remote site, the generator is the cheap part. The real costs are fuel delivered rather than fuel bought, convoys, site visits, noise, heat and exhaust, fuel theft, emissions, and downtime when the generator stops. Autonomous power is not maintenance-free. Diesel is still the right tool for short projects on accessible sites, very heavy or unpredictable loads, and genuine emergencies. Argues that the better comparison is dependency, not 'solar versus diesel'.

---

### Designing power from the load backwards

URL: https://www.melrakki.systems/resilience/designing-power-from-the-load-backwards/
Published: 2026-09-22

The sizing method, in order. Characterise the load and its duty cycle. Turn it into daily watt-hours (100 W continuous is 2.4 kWh a day). Account for losses: Harka Solar's 9.6 kWh nameplate gives about 7.5 kWh of real work. Set the reserve needed with no input. Match generation to the worst month's peak sun hours, not the average. Let the result decide the tier: solar-only where the worst month closes, hybrid where it does not. Ends with the nine numbers to bring to a first conversation.
